status: Pilot, written by Claude on 12 November 2026 and not yet checked by the translation workers. The polite 요 form throughout, except where the dictionary form is the lesson.

lessons.title: Sounds and Script - Letters Built into Blocks, Part 1
lessons.description: Korean letters are stacked into blocks, one block for each beat. The block 한 is three letters together: ㅎ, ㅏ, and ㄴ.

lessons.title: Sounds and Script - Plain, Breathy, and Tight, Part 1
lessons.description: Korean has three kinds of some sounds: plain, breathy, and tight. Hear 불 against 풀, and 달 against 딸.

lessons.title: Sounds and Script - Two O Sounds, Part 1
lessons.description: Korean has two sounds where English has one o: the open ㅓ and the rounded ㅗ. Hear 거기 against 고기, and 커피 against 코피.

lessons.title: Sounds and Script - The Sound Underneath, Part 1
lessons.description: A block can end in a consonant written underneath it. One beginning, 바, with four different endings makes four words.

lessons.title: Patterns - The Verb Never Says Who, Part 1
lessons.description: The verb is the same whoever is going: 가요. Only the word in front, marked by 는 or 은, says who.

lessons.title: Patterns - Polite Endings, Part 1
lessons.description: The ending of the verb says when it happens: 가요 for now, 갔어요 for done, and 갈 거예요 for still to come. A no is 안 in front.

lessons.title: Patterns - Dictionary Form and Polite Form, Part 1
lessons.description: A dictionary lists every verb ending in 다. To say it politely to someone, the 다 comes off and an ending in 요 goes on.

lessons.title: Patterns - Counting Words, Part 1
lessons.description: The thing comes first, then the number, then a counting word that fits it: 명 for people, 권 for books, 마리 for animals, 대 for machines.

lessons.title: Sentence Building - The Verb Comes Last, Part 1
lessons.description: English says I eat rice. Korean says I rice eat: 는 marks who, 을 or 를 marks what, and the verb closes the sentence.

lessons.title: Sentence Building - Asking a Question, Part 1
lessons.description: In polite speech, a question has the same words in the same order as the statement. Only the voice rises.
words: This is the bus to Seoul.
Is this the bus to Seoul?

lessons.title: Sentence Building - Saying No, Part 1
lessons.description: To say something is not so, put 안 in front of the verb. Nothing else in the sentence changes.

lessons.title: Sentence Building - Little Words After, Part 1
lessons.description: Where English puts to, at, with, and by in front of a word, Korean puts a little marker after it: 에, 에서, 와, 로.

lessons.title: Sentences in Use - Going Places, Part 1
lessons.description: The verb 가요, to go, at work in whole sentences. The place comes first, marked by 에, and the verb comes last.
words: I am going to the market.
We are going to the beach.
Are you going to the party?

lessons.title: Sentences in Use - Questions and Answers, Part 1
lessons.description: A question and its answer, side by side. Korean says I have a car as a car exists: 차가 있어요.

lessons.title: Sentences in Use - Describing Things, Part 1
lessons.description: Korean describing words behave like verbs: they close the sentence themselves, with no word for is.

lessons.title: Sentences in Use - Yesterday, Today, and Tomorrow, Part 1
lessons.description: One trip to the market, told three ways. Only the end of the verb changes: 갔어요, 가요, 갈 거예요.
words: I went to the market yesterday.
I am going to the market today.
I will go to the market tomorrow.
